titleText.es: Los niños son experimentos genéticos. ¡Lo único que hacemos es experimentar de forma responsable!
titleText.en: Kids are genetic experiments.  We're just experimenting responsibly!
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text and the official English image title make the same joke about treating children as genetic experiments while claiming that the experimentation is responsible; the English text preserves the official two-space sentence break.

applications.explanationEn: Bebidas names the things first, and the neutral description azucaradas follows it.
Azucaradas ends in -as to match the feminine plural noun bebidas.
Intentas changes for one familiar listener, provocar remains in its unchanged -ar form with attached le, and diabetes fills the attempted action's result slot.
Le attaches to the end of the unchanged verb provocar and identifies the person affected.
Context identifies le as the daughter; the condition caused in her is named immediately afterward.

regions.labelEs: SÍ. LUEGO, SI ALGO SALE MAL, LE CORTAMOS EL SUMINISTRO DE INSULINA.

applications.explanationEn: Si introduces a genuinely possible condition, and sale uses the ordinary present form; algo is the condition's subject between them.
Sale is the singular present form of salir for the situation, and mal marks its bad outcome.

applications.exampleEs: LE CORTAMOS EL SUMINISTRO DE INSULINA
applications.explanationEn: Le identifies the daughter as the person affected, while Spanish keeps the masculine article el before the complete item phrase suministro de insulina.
Because le has already identified the daughter, el introduces suministro as her supply while agreeing with that masculine singular noun.
Here de names the substance supplied, not a general purpose or field.

regions.labelEs: USO EL PARADIGMA PARQUE JURÁSICO DE PATERNIDAD.

applications.explanationEn: Parque is the masculine singular noun, and the descriptive word jurásico follows it in the Spanish title.
Jurásico uses masculine singular -o to match parque.
Here de introduces paternidad as the field to which the stated paradigm is being applied.

cards.noteEn: Más can describe a greater amount or degree, or stand alone when the missing person or thing is clear. It keeps its written accent; mas without an accent is a different, literary word meaning 'but.'
Bebidas is the feminine plural noun for things people drink.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Azucaradas describes feminine plural things that contain sugar or have had sugar added.
Intentas is the present form of intentar for one familiar person. Follow it directly with an unchanged action verb to say what that person tries to do.

example.en: Are you trying to open the window?

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.answerEn: to cause something in someone; to give someone a condition
cards.noteEn: Provocarle combines provocar with attached le. The result or condition is named separately, while le identifies one person affected by it; a later phrase beginning with a can clarify that person.

example.es: El polvo puede provocarle tos a Luis.
example.en: The dust can give Luis a cough.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Small words naming who or what receives the action can attach directly: conocer and te become conocerte, and ayudar and me become ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: Why does calling this a ‘Jurassic Park’ parenting approach make the plan darkly comic?
cards.answerEn: Jurassic Park's engineered dinosaurs were supposed to depend on a supplied nutrient as a containment safeguard; the parent proposes creating a medical dependency and controlling the matching supply.
cards.noteEn: In the story, the dinosaurs' engineered lysine dependence is meant to keep them under control if they escape. Deliberately causing diabetes and then controlling access to insulin turns that fictional contingency plan into an alarming parenting policy.
Diabetes is normally a feminine noun in Spanish: la diabetes.
Unaccented si introduces a condition or possibility. With an opening y in a question, ¿y si...? invites someone to consider 'what if ...?' This differs from accented sí, 'yes.'

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.
Algo refers to an unspecified thing. English often uses “anything” in a question even though Spanish still uses algo. It does not change for the thing's gender or number.
Salir normally means “to leave” or “to go out,” but with a calculation or attempt it can describe the result that comes out.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a plan, attempt, or situation goes wrong or turns out badly?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of salir followed by mal.
cards.noteEn: Salir changes for person and time, while mal stays unchanged: sale mal, salió mal, or puede salir mal. This use describes an outcome, not physical movement out of a place.

cards.answerEn: badly; poorly; wrong (describing how an action is done)
cards.noteEn: After an action, mal describes the way it is performed. Natural English may use ‘badly,’ ‘poorly,’ or ‘wrong’ depending on the action.

cards.answerEn: marks one person or entity affected by what happens
cards.noteEn: Le can identify the person whose body, possessions, or situation is affected, even when nothing is literally given to them. It can refer to him, her, or formal you. English may use 'his,' 'her,' 'your,' or 'to' or 'with' that person; the surrounding words identify who is meant.

example.es: Le lavé las manos al niño.

cards.promptEs: me arreglan el móvil · van a lavarle el coche
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish identify the person affected through a body part, possession, or other closely connected noun without putting a possessive word before it?
cards.answerEn: Mark the affected person with me, te, le, nos, or les, then use el, la, los, or las before the closely connected noun.
cards.noteEn: The short person word goes before a changed verb, as in le repararon, or attaches to an unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form, as in repararle. The article matches the related noun, whether it names a body part, possession, service, or closely associated aspect. Natural English often expresses that relationship with my, your, his, her, our, or their.

example.es: Van a lavarle el coche a Ana.
example.en: They are going to wash Ana's car.

cards.answerEn: we cut off; we discontinue; we cut off (completed past)
cards.noteEn: Cortamos is the nosotros form of cortar in both the present and the completed past. With a service, supply, cable, or connection, cortar can mean stopping or disconnecting it rather than literally slicing it; context shows the time intended.

example.es: Ayer cortamos el servicio durante una hora.
example.en: Yesterday we cut off the service for an hour.

cards.answerEn: the; English often uses my, your, or another owner's word
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el before a masculine singular body part or close possession when me, te, le, or the surrounding context already identifies the affected owner. El matches the thing, not its owner's gender; it does not itself say whose it is.

De can connect a container, area, food, or supply to what it contains. It names the contents or ingredients, not the container's material or its owner. English may use 'of' or put the content word first.

example.en: She brought a bag of sweets.

cards.noteEn: Insulina is a feminine noun for the hormone and medicine used to control blood sugar.

example.es: La insulina regula el azúcar en la sangre.

cards.noteEn: A paradigma is a model or general way of understanding and approaching something. Despite its final -a, it is masculine: el paradigma.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to its type, purpose, or field
cards.noteEn: Spanish often puts de between two nouns where English puts the describing noun first. In una silla de oficina, oficina tells you the chair's intended use. This is different from de naming an owner, material, contents, or a part's larger whole.
Paternidad can name the state of being a parent or the work and approach involved in raising children.

example.es: El curso trata sobre la paternidad.
